newsitem.title: INDIA: India proposal on edible oil not to hit market now.
newsitem.headline: India proposal on edible oil not to hit market now.

text.p: An increase in India's import duties on edible oil will not immediately hit the domestic market but prices will surge with the onset of the lean season in July, industry officials said on Thursday.
Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra said on Wednesday he had written to Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposing that the import duty on edible oils be increased to 30 percent from 20 percent.

Mishra told reporters after a meeting with state agriculture ministers in the Indian capital that he had received complaints from industry officials that edible oil imports were cheaper than domestic production.

"Even if the duties are increased it will not immediately affect the market because the summer crop has started moving," Navinbhai Shah, president of Bombay Oilseeds and Oil Exchange Ltd, told Reuters.
"But prices will shoot up once the lean season starts in July," Shah said.
The months of July to October are considered lean months because domestic supplies dry up as demand surges due to the Hindu festival season.

India harvests two oilseed crops annually, with the bulk of its output from the winter crop. The winter crop is sown in July and harvest starts from October. The summer crop harvest starts from March.
The Agriculture Ministry has set a output target of 9.5 million tonnes of summer oilseeds.
Mishra did not indicate whether Chidambaram had replied to his request to raise duties.

Malaysian palm olein prices eased on Tuesday on news of Mishra's proposal to raise edible oil import duties by 10 percent. Malaysian traders said it would make Malaysian palm olein prices more expensive and might reduce buying by India.
Chicago soy oil futures also suffered losses on the news.
Industry officials said increasing the import duties would affect the domestic market as the 1996/97 oilseeds crop was expected to be around 21 million tonnes compared with 22 million in 1995/96.
"It is not the proper time to consider a rise in duty as the crop is expected to be less than the last year," Shah said.

O.P. Goenka, president of the Central Organisation of Oil Industry and Trade (COOIT), said: "Imports are not going to be affected because the demand is rising due to increases in per capita income and annual growth in population of two percent."
"If the duties are increased domestic prices will go up by 2,000 ($56) to 3,000 rupees per tonne, but after two to three months," Goenka said.
He said edible oil imports are expected to rise to 1.5 million tonnes in 1996/97 compared with 1.2 million last year.

"I don't think there will be a hike in the edible oil import duties because, under the Common Minimum Programme of the government, the consumer comes first, then the farmer and then the industry," said one analyst who asked not to be identified. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
